source.filename: Stiffness-Tuneable Segment for Continuum Soft Robots.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is assumed to be inextensible due to its Young's modulus being significantly higher than that of the silicone membrane
Initial friction between flaps in the normal unjammed state is assumed to be zero
Tensile stiffness of the single nylon thread is modeled linearly based on its Young's modulus, length, and circular cross-sectional area
Tensile stiffness of the silicone membrane is modeled linearly using its Young's modulus, total length, and combined inner/outer cross-sectional area
Flap-silicone membrane interface is modeled via linear shear modulus of silicone considering Poisson's ratio
Flap-flap interface geometry is approximated as an isosceles trapezoid to determine first and second area moments of inertia
Euler-Bernoulli beam theory under cantilevered conditions is assumed for the layer structure deflection
Flap-nylon interface stiffness is assumed to be negligible relative to flap-flap and flap-membrane shear stiffnesses in the jammed state
Flap-flap and flap-membrane shear stiffnesses are assumed to be approximately equal within a specific pressure range
Incomplete contact between flaps and between flap and membrane is accounted for using empirical reduction factors (alpha and beta)
control_variables: Flap geometric parameters (flap length L, flap width W, flap thickness H = 0.23 mm, distance between bilateral flaps h, central angle phi)
Layer assembly parameters (slot length D, hole-slot center distance d, segment diameter phi, overlap count of 6.5 layers per side)
Material properties (PET film with friction coefficient 0.4, Dragon Skin 10 silicone membrane of 0.3 mm thickness, 0.108 mm diameter nylon thread)

Vertebra and spine parameters (vertebra diameter Dv, vertebra height Wv, gap between vertebrae Gv, total vertebrae length 76 mm, 10 mm end supports, rigid-to-overall length ratio <= 50%, Ecoflex 00-50 silicone SCR body, ABS vertebrae)
Deflection and compression testing displacement increments (2 cm increments up to 10 cm)
Number of loading cycles (50 cycles per testing protocol)
dependent_variables: Deflection force and axial compression force (N)
Central diameter retention ratio under bending

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A tubular stiffening segment utilizing layer jamming can temporarily increase soft robot stiffness under negative pressure, producing an increase in bending stiffness of over 15x at 0 degrees, over 30x at 90 degrees, and up to 60x in compressive stiffness at -60 kPa.

A bio-inspired flexible spine featuring rigid ABS vertebrae integrated with an elastomeric soft continuum robot prevents cross-sectional buckling and maintains segment diameter during bending (achieving a diameter ratio of 0.981 at 180 degrees compared to 0.856 for an unreinforced soft continuum robot).

An analytical mechanics model dividing layer jamming shear behavior into pre-slip, transition, and full-slip regimes captures the effective stiffness variation with applied vacuum pressure, achieving a minimum determination coefficient (R^2) of 0.9525 relative to experimental data.

The tuneable-stiffness soft continuum robot demonstrates an adjustable length range of 185.35 mm to 363.35 mm, a bending angle reaching 196 degrees, and peak load support of 31.45 N under operational pressures of +/-60 kPa.

experimental_setup: Mechanical test bench comprising an axially moving slide, a linear actuator, and a digital force sensor (WD-500, Aidebao Co)
Aluminum plate mounting fixture securing the TSCR relative to the actuator and force sensor
Two-stage vacuum pump (VP 280) supplying vacuum pressure between 0 kPa and -60 kPa in -20 kPa steps through a 6 mm PVC pipe
Lateral bending deflection testing setup at 0-degree and 90-degree configurations tested at 2 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm, and 10 cm displacements for 50 cycles
Axial compression testing setup on the straight TSCR evaluated from 0 cm to 10 cm displacement in 2 cm steps for 50 cycles
Manual bending angle evaluation from 0 degrees to 180 degrees in 45-degree increments to measure central diameter changes using photographic comparison
future_work: Miniaturization of the TSCR for interventional medicine applications
Application of the current TSCR design to exoskeleton rehabilitation robots
Designing biomimetic flaps inspired by scaled organisms such as pangolins and fish to improve the trade-off between rigidity and flexibility
Investigation of alternative flap weaving patterns and materials
Quantifying the hysteresis effect of stiffening segment loading and unloading for TSCR controller development
independent_variables: Applied vacuum pressure (0 kPa, -20 kPa, -40 kPa, -60 kPa)
Bending configuration angle (0 degrees, 45 degrees, 90 degrees, 135 degrees, 180 degrees)
Imposed displacement during lateral deflection and axial compression (0 to 10 cm in 2 cm increments)
Structural configuration (tuneable-stiffness soft continuum robot with vertebrae vs. soft continuum robot without vertebrae)
limitations_inferred: Empirical calibration parameters (alpha and beta) are required to fit the analytical model to experimental results, limiting purely analytical first-principles prediction for uncalibrated geometries
Central diameter evaluation relies on discrete manual bending and photographic inspection rather than continuous dynamic non-contact measurement
Cyclic endurance and fatigue life of the thin silicone membranes and PET flaps under prolonged cycling beyond 50 cycles are not documented
The interaction between simultaneous internal pneumatic spine actuation and vacuum layer jamming was not fully characterized under closed-loop control
limitations_stated_by_authors: The stiffening segment bends under compressive force and exhibits unstable behavior caused by sudden slip between flaps
The TSCR exhibits a tendency to buckle under compression, though deformation is reversible upon releasing vacuum
Nylon threads constrain flap displacement at the length limits of the stiffening segment

Discrepancies between theoretical predictions and experimental results occur due to small manufacturing defects in the silicone membrane, irregular flap stacking, small gas leaks, and non-uniform negative pressure distribution
The stiffening segment imposes a certain limit on compliance
Hysteresis during loading and unloading of the stiffening segment must be accounted for and quantified for control systems
The current TSCR scale requires miniaturization before it can be applied to interventional medicine
main_results: Under lateral bending at 0 degrees, TSCR bending stiffness increased by more than 15x, with maximum average deflection force reaching 5 N
Under lateral bending at 90 degrees, TSCR bending stiffness increased by more than 30x, reaching an average maximum deflection force of 31 N
In axial compression, TSCR stiffness increased up to 60x in the jammed state relative to the initial unjammed TSCR, reaching an average compression force of 64 N
The central diameter ratio at 180-degree bending was maintained at 0.981 for the TSCR, outperforming the unreinforced SCR which buckled at a ratio of 0.856
The stiffening segment achieved an adjustable length range from 185.35 mm to 363.35 mm and a maximum bending angle of 196 degrees
The analytical layer jamming model matched experimental lateral bending data at 90 degrees with a minimum R^2 of 0.9525
Finite element predictions showed close alignment with the analytical model and experimental results
modeling_methods: Minimal analytical mechanics model for structural layer jamming of two-layer and extended N-layer flap systems
Euler-Bernoulli beam theory applied under cantilevered conditions to evaluate layer structure deflection and effective shear stiffness
Piecewise shear interface modeling divided into three distinct operational regimes: pre-slip regime, transition regime, and full-slip regime
Lumped series and parallel spring stiffness combinations for flap-flap, flap-membrane, flap-nylon, and membrane tensile stiffness components
Finite element analysis of TSCR mechanical behavior
performance_metrics: Deflection force (N) and axial compression force (N)
Stiffening coefficient gamma (ratio of average jammed force to average unjammed force)
Central diameter ratio relative to initial 0-degree diameter
Coefficient of determination (R^2) between theoretical model predictions and experimental measurements
possible_gap_implications: The finding that embedding internal rigid vertebrae mitigates the classic cross-sectional buckling and stiffness degradation of curved layer-jamming segments suggests a design path for continuum robots requiring high payload capacity in bent configurations, but does not prove novelty over all prior variable-stiffness continuum architectures

The persistence of sudden inter-layer slip and unmodeled loading-unloading hysteresis indicates that predictive, dynamic closed-loop control of hybrid soft-rigid jamming manipulators remains an unresolved research challenge
paper.research_objective: To design, model, and experimentally evaluate a tuneable-stiffness soft continuum robot (TSCR) that integrates a layer-jamming tubular stiffening segment with a bio-inspired flexible drivable spine to achieve reversible stiffness tuning, shape control, and prevention of buckling during bending.
paper.research_problem: Soft continuum robots lack structural stiffness when manipulating objects compared to rigid robots, leading to large undesired deformations from small interaction forces, while existing cylindrical layer-jamming stiffening segments suffer from cross-sectional deformation and buckling during bending that reduces overall stiffness.
paper.title: Stiffness-Tuneable Segment for Continuum Soft Robots with Vertebrae
